case_info.scenario: A 20-year-old man presented with bilateral neck masses that gradually increased in size for over 5 months following a red cross tattoo on his anterior neck. Three months after the tattoo, the red ink spontaneously faded and was replaced by atrophic scars and necrotic ulcers with light bloody exudation. Initial management with antibiotics and topical corticosteroids yielded no improvement. Physical examination revealed firm, ill-defined cervical and submental lymphadenopathy bilaterally, alongside a midline anterior neck mass demonstrating cutaneous invasion, ulceration, and crusting (Figure 1A). No systemic symptom was observed. Laboratory tests including complete blood cell count, tuberculosis T-cell gamma interferon assay, serum IgG4, and complete immune testing results were within normal limits. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated ill-defined infiltrative masses measuring 3.8 × 2.9 cm and 3.4 × 4.2 cm on both sides of the neck and 4.9 × 3.5 cm in the suprasternal fossa. The lesions showed heterogeneous iso-/hyperintense signal on T1-weighted imaging and hyper-/hypointense signal on T2-weighted imaging, with contrast-enhanced lesions showing predominantly peripheral enhancement. The internal jugular vein in the lower part of the neck was invisible, leaving vague hyperintense signal embedded in the mass (Figure 1B). Enhanced computed tomography implied bilateral internal jugular vein thrombosis as well. Repeated fine-needle aspiration yielded necrotic debris, eosinophilic and lymphocyte-dominated inflammation, and fibrosis, which were insufficient for a definitive diagnosis. Given concern regarding the radiographic features and clinical progression, surgical excision with bilateral internal jugular vein ligation and free rectus femoris flap reconstruction was performed.

case_info.explanation: C. Tattoo-associated necrotizing granulomatous lymphadenitis Histopathological examination showed reactive lymphoid hyperplasia with extensive necrosis, chronic inflammatory cell infiltration (predominantly lymphocytes and plasma cells), and noncaseating granuloma formation. The histological features of inflammatory emboli in the internal jugular vein are similar with that of cervical lymph nodes (Figure 2). Immunohistochemical staining revealed SMA-positive myofibroblastoma cells, but pan-cytokeratin, IgG4, S-100, SOX10, and CD34 were negative. Acid-fast bacilli staining was negative, and mycobacterium tuberculosis PCR failed to detect mycobacterial DNA. Epstein-Barr virus–encoded RNA staining was negative. These findings collectively supported a diagnosis of necrotizing granulomatous lymphadenitis. Tattooing has emerged as a modern cultural phenomenon associated with personal expression. However, its potential adverse effects, ranging from infections to neoplastic complications, demand heightened clinical awareness. Emerging evidence suggests a possible association between tattoos and malignant neoplasms such as lymphoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and basal cell carcinoma, with a higher incidence observed in tattooed populations.1 Granulomatous reactions to tattoo pigments, typically classified as delayed hypersensitivity responses, manifest histopathologically as granuloma annulare or perforating granulomas confined to tattooed regions.2Clinically, these present as pruritic, erythematous nodules or lichenoid changes, rarely extending into deeper tissues.3Heavy metals (eg, mercury, cadmium) and organic dyes (notably red pigments) in tattoo pigments are implicated in triggering delayed-type hypersensitivity or foreign-body granulomas. While pigment deposition within lesions is a consistent histopathological hallmark, necrosis remains uncommon, with only one other reported case, to our knowledge.4 Lymphatic migration of tattoo pigments may result in lymphadenopathy characterized by painless enlargement and intranodal pigment accumulation, often mimicking metastasis. Imaging modalities such as positron emission tomography–computed tomography frequently fail to differentiate pigment-laden nodes from malignant metastasis, underscoring the necessity of meticulous tattoo history documentation and histopathologic confirmation.5Furthermore, hematogenous dissemination of pigments to distant organs (eg, liver) has been reported, potentially leading to misdiagnosis as metastatic melanoma, particularly in high-risk cohorts.6 Unlike conventional granulomatous reactions, this patient exhibited aggressive local invasion, deep cervical lymphadenopathy, and jugular inflammatory thrombus in the absence of systemic symptoms or infectious etiologies. Thrombus formation in benign inflammatory contexts is previously reported only in association with invasive infections or malignant neoplasms. We propose 3 potential mechanisms: (1) venous wall erosion secondary to granulomatous lymphadenitis, (2) a hypercoagulable state induced by chronic inflammation and cytokine dysregulation (eg, IL-6-mediated fibrinogen production), and (3) vascular stasis due to mass compression by enlarged lymph nodes. This case distinguishes from prior reports of necrotizing granulomas confined to the tattooed skin with minimal deep infiltration. Lymph node involvement preceded local skin reactions, which favored the diagnosis. Notably, red tattoo pigment was absent in resected lesions despite histopathological and clinical correlation supporting the diagnosis. This report expands the spectrum of tattoo-associated pathology. Clinicians should remain highly suspicious of tattoo-related etiologies in patients presenting with necrotic neck masses, even in the absence of visible pigment. Vascular invasion necessitates urgent evaluation, as thrombosis may require immediate intervention. While topical corticosteroid therapy proves ineffective, complete surgical excision remains the cornerstone of both diagnosis and management. The patient finally recovered under the comprehensive treatment mode of surgical operation, short-term systemic hormone therapy, and infection prevention.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

Enhanced computed tomography implied bilateral internal jugular vein thrombosis as well. Repeated fine-needle aspiration yielded necrotic debris, eosinophilic and lymphocyte-dominated inflammation, and fibrosis, which were insufficient for a definitive diagnosis. case_info.explanation: C. Tattoo-associated necrotizing granulomatous lymphadenitis Histopathological examination showed reactive lymphoid hyperplasia with extensive necrosis, chronic inflammatory cell infiltration (predominantly lymphocytes and plasma cells), and noncaseating granuloma formation. The histological features of inflammatory emboli in the internal jugular vein are similar with that of cervical lymph nodes (Figure 2). Immunohistochemical staining revealed SMA-positive myofibroblastoma cells, but pan-cytokeratin, IgG4, S-100, SOX10, and CD34 were negative. Acid-fast bacilli staining was negative, and mycobacterium tuberculosis PCR failed to detect mycobacterial DNA. Epstein-Barr virus–encoded RNA staining was negative. These findings collectively supported a diagnosis of necrotizing granulomatous lymphadenitis. Tattooing has emerged as a modern cultural phenomenon associated with personal expression. However, its potential adverse effects, ranging from infections to neoplastic complications, demand heightened clinical awareness. Emerging evidence suggests a possible association between tattoos and malignant neoplasms such as lymphoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and basal cell carcinoma, with a higher incidence observed in tattooed populations.1 Granulomatous reactions to tattoo pigments, typically classified as delayed hypersensitivity responses, manifest histopathologically as granuloma annulare or perforating granulomas confined to tattooed regions.2Clinically, these present as pruritic, erythematous nodules or lichenoid changes, rarely extending into deeper tissues.3Heavy metals (eg, mercury, cadmium) and organic dyes (notably red pigments) in tattoo pigments are implicated in triggering delayed-type hypersensitivity or foreign-body granulomas. While pigment deposition within lesions is a consistent histopathological hallmark, necrosis remains uncommon, with only one other reported case, to our knowledge.4 Lymphatic migration of tattoo pigments may result in lymphadenopathy characterized by painless enlargement and intranodal pigment accumulation, often mimicking metastasis. Imaging modalities such as positron emission tomography–computed tomography frequently fail to differentiate pigment-laden nodes from malignant metastasis, underscoring the necessity of meticulous tattoo history documentation and histopathologic confirmation.5Furthermore, hematogenous dissemination of pigments to distant organs (eg, liver) has been reported, potentially leading to misdiagnosis as metastatic melanoma, particularly in high-risk cohorts.6 Unlike conventional granulomatous reactions, this patient exhibited aggressive local invasion, deep cervical lymphadenopathy, and jugular inflammatory thrombus in the absence of systemic symptoms or infectious etiologies. Thrombus formation in benign inflammatory contexts is previously reported only in association with invasive infections or malignant neoplasms. We propose 3 potential mechanisms: (1) venous wall erosion secondary to granulomatous lymphadenitis, (2) a hypercoagulable state induced by chronic inflammation and cytokine dysregulation (eg, IL-6-mediated fibrinogen production), and (3) vascular stasis due to mass compression by enlarged lymph nodes. This case distinguishes from prior reports of necrotizing granulomas confined to the tattooed skin with minimal deep infiltration. Lymph node involvement preceded local skin reactions, which favored the diagnosis. Notably, red tattoo pigment was absent in resected lesions despite histopathological and clinical correlation supporting the diagnosis. This report expands the spectrum of tattoo-associated pathology. Clinicians should remain highly suspicious of tattoo-related etiologies in patients presenting with necrotic neck masses, even in the absence of visible pigment. Vascular invasion necessitates urgent evaluation, as thrombosis may require immediate intervention. While topical corticosteroid therapy proves ineffective, complete surgical excision remains the cornerstone of both diagnosis and management. The patient finally recovered under the comprehensive treatment mode of surgical operation, short-term systemic hormone therapy, and infection prevention.

   Scoring:

       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."

       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also

   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.

case_info.explanation: C. Tattoo-associated necrotizing granulomatous lymphadenitis Histopathological examination showed reactive lymphoid hyperplasia with extensive necrosis, chronic inflammatory cell infiltration (predominantly lymphocytes and plasma cells), and noncaseating granuloma formation. The histological features of inflammatory emboli in the internal jugular vein are similar with that of cervical lymph nodes (Figure 2). Immunohistochemical staining revealed SMA-positive myofibroblastoma cells, but pan-cytokeratin, IgG4, S-100, SOX10, and CD34 were negative. Acid-fast bacilli staining was negative, and mycobacterium tuberculosis PCR failed to detect mycobacterial DNA. Epstein-Barr virus–encoded RNA staining was negative. These findings collectively supported a diagnosis of necrotizing granulomatous lymphadenitis. Tattooing has emerged as a modern cultural phenomenon associated with personal expression. However, its potential adverse effects, ranging from infections to neoplastic complications, demand heightened clinical awareness. Emerging evidence suggests a possible association between tattoos and malignant neoplasms such as lymphoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and basal cell carcinoma, with a higher incidence observed in tattooed populations.1 Granulomatous reactions to tattoo pigments, typically classified as delayed hypersensitivity responses, manifest histopathologically as granuloma annulare or perforating granulomas confined to tattooed regions.2Clinically, these present as pruritic, erythematous nodules or lichenoid changes, rarely extending into deeper tissues.3Heavy metals (eg, mercury, cadmium) and organic dyes (notably red pigments) in tattoo pigments are implicated in triggering delayed-type hypersensitivity or foreign-body granulomas. While pigment deposition within lesions is a consistent histopathological hallmark, necrosis remains uncommon, with only one other reported case, to our knowledge.4 Lymphatic migration of tattoo pigments may result in lymphadenopathy characterized by painless enlargement and intranodal pigment accumulation, often mimicking metastasis. Imaging modalities such as positron emission tomography–computed tomography frequently fail to differentiate pigment-laden nodes from malignant metastasis, underscoring the necessity of meticulous tattoo history documentation and histopathologic confirmation.5Furthermore, hematogenous dissemination of pigments to distant organs (eg, liver) has been reported, potentially leading to misdiagnosis as metastatic melanoma, particularly in high-risk cohorts.6 Unlike conventional granulomatous reactions, this patient exhibited aggressive local invasion, deep cervical lymphadenopathy, and jugular inflammatory thrombus in the absence of systemic symptoms or infectious etiologies. Thrombus formation in benign inflammatory contexts is previously reported only in association with invasive infections or malignant neoplasms. We propose 3 potential mechanisms: (1) venous wall erosion secondary to granulomatous lymphadenitis, (2) a hypercoagulable state induced by chronic inflammation and cytokine dysregulation (eg, IL-6-mediated fibrinogen production), and (3) vascular stasis due to mass compression by enlarged lymph nodes. This case distinguishes from prior reports of necrotizing granulomas confined to the tattooed skin with minimal deep infiltration. Lymph node involvement preceded local skin reactions, which favored the diagnosis. Notably, red tattoo pigment was absent in resected lesions despite histopathological and clinical correlation supporting the diagnosis. This report expands the spectrum of tattoo-associated pathology. Clinicians should remain highly suspicious of tattoo-related etiologies in patients presenting with necrotic neck masses, even in the absence of visible pigment. Vascular invasion necessitates urgent evaluation, as thrombosis may require immediate intervention. While topical corticosteroid therapy proves ineffective, complete surgical excision remains the cornerstone of both diagnosis and management. The patient finally recovered under the comprehensive treatment mode of surgical operation, short-term systemic hormone therapy, and infection prevention.

While pigment deposition within lesions is a consistent histopathological hallmark, necrosis remains uncommon, with only one other reported case, to our knowledge.4 Lymphatic migration of tattoo pigments may result in lymphadenopathy characterized by painless enlargement and intranodal pigment accumulation, often mimicking metastasis. Imaging modalities such as positron emission tomography–computed tomography frequently fail to differentiate pigment-laden nodes from malignant metastasis, underscoring the necessity of meticulous tattoo history documentation and histopathologic confirmation.5Furthermore, hematogenous dissemination of pigments to distant organs (eg, liver) has been reported, potentially leading to misdiagnosis as metastatic melanoma, particularly in high-risk cohorts.6 Unlike conventional granulomatous reactions, this patient exhibited aggressive local invasion, deep cervical lymphadenopathy, and jugular inflammatory thrombus in the absence of systemic symptoms or infectious etiologies. While topical corticosteroid therapy proves ineffective, complete surgical excision remains the cornerstone of both diagnosis and management. The patient finally recovered under the comprehensive treatment mode of surgical operation, short-term systemic hormone therapy, and infection prevention.

case_info.explanation: C. Tattoo-associated necrotizing granulomatous lymphadenitis Histopathological examination showed reactive lymphoid hyperplasia with extensive necrosis, chronic inflammatory cell infiltration (predominantly lymphocytes and plasma cells), and noncaseating granuloma formation. The histological features of inflammatory emboli in the internal jugular vein are similar with that of cervical lymph nodes (Figure 2). Immunohistochemical staining revealed SMA-positive myofibroblastoma cells, but pan-cytokeratin, IgG4, S-100, SOX10, and CD34 were negative. Acid-fast bacilli staining was negative, and mycobacterium tuberculosis PCR failed to detect mycobacterial DNA. Epstein-Barr virus–encoded RNA staining was negative. These findings collectively supported a diagnosis of necrotizing granulomatous lymphadenitis. Tattooing has emerged as a modern cultural phenomenon associated with personal expression. However, its potential adverse effects, ranging from infections to neoplastic complications, demand heightened clinical awareness. Emerging evidence suggests a possible association between tattoos and malignant neoplasms such as lymphoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and basal cell carcinoma, with a higher incidence observed in tattooed populations.1 Granulomatous reactions to tattoo pigments, typically classified as delayed hypersensitivity responses, manifest histopathologically as granuloma annulare or perforating granulomas confined to tattooed regions.2Clinically, these present as pruritic, erythematous nodules or lichenoid changes, rarely extending into deeper tissues.3Heavy metals (eg, mercury, cadmium) and organic dyes (notably red pigments) in tattoo pigments are implicated in triggering delayed-type hypersensitivity or foreign-body granulomas. While pigment deposition within lesions is a consistent histopathological hallmark, necrosis remains uncommon, with only one other reported case, to our knowledge.4 Lymphatic migration of tattoo pigments may result in lymphadenopathy characterized by painless enlargement and intranodal pigment accumulation, often mimicking metastasis. Imaging modalities such as positron emission tomography–computed tomography frequently fail to differentiate pigment-laden nodes from malignant metastasis, underscoring the necessity of meticulous tattoo history documentation and histopathologic confirmation.5Furthermore, hematogenous dissemination of pigments to distant organs (eg, liver) has been reported, potentially leading to misdiagnosis as metastatic melanoma, particularly in high-risk cohorts.6 Unlike conventional granulomatous reactions, this patient exhibited aggressive local invasion, deep cervical lymphadenopathy, and jugular inflammatory thrombus in the absence of systemic symptoms or infectious etiologies. Thrombus formation in benign inflammatory contexts is previously reported only in association with invasive infections or malignant neoplasms. We propose 3 potential mechanisms: (1) venous wall erosion secondary to granulomatous lymphadenitis, (2) a hypercoagulable state induced by chronic inflammation and cytokine dysregulation (eg, IL-6-mediated fibrinogen production), and (3) vascular stasis due to mass compression by enlarged lymph nodes. This case distinguishes from prior reports of necrotizing granulomas confined to the tattooed skin with minimal deep infiltration. Lymph node involvement preceded local skin reactions, which favored the diagnosis. Notably, red tattoo pigment was absent in resected lesions despite histopathological and clinical correlation supporting the diagnosis. This report expands the spectrum of tattoo-associated pathology. Clinicians should remain highly suspicious of tattoo-related etiologies in patients presenting with necrotic neck masses, even in the absence of visible pigment. Vascular invasion necessitates urgent evaluation, as thrombosis may require immediate intervention. While topical corticosteroid therapy proves ineffective, complete surgical excision remains the cornerstone of both diagnosis and management. The patient finally recovered under the comprehensive treatment mode of surgical operation, short-term systemic hormone therapy, and infection prevention.

[Clinical case]
A 20-year-old man presented with bilateral neck masses that gradually increased in size for over 5 months following a red cross tattoo on his anterior neck. Three months after the tattoo, the red ink spontaneously faded and was replaced by atrophic scars and necrotic ulcers with light bloody exudation. Initial management with antibiotics and topical corticosteroids yielded no improvement. Physical examination revealed firm, ill-defined cervical and submental lymphadenopathy bilaterally, alongside a midline anterior neck mass demonstrating cutaneous invasion, ulceration, and crusting (Figure 1A). No systemic symptom was observed. Laboratory tests including complete blood cell count, tuberculosis T-cell gamma interferon assay, serum IgG4, and complete immune testing results were within normal limits. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated ill-defined infiltrative masses measuring 3.8 × 2.9 cm and 3.4 × 4.2 cm on both sides of the neck and 4.9 × 3.5 cm in the suprasternal fossa. The lesions showed heterogeneous iso-/hyperintense signal on T1-weighted imaging and hyper-/hypointense signal on T2-weighted imaging, with contrast-enhanced lesions showing predominantly peripheral enhancement. The internal jugular vein in the lower part of the neck was invisible, leaving vague hyperintense signal embedded in the mass (Figure 1B). Enhanced computed tomography implied bilateral internal jugular vein thrombosis as well. Repeated fine-needle aspiration yielded necrotic debris, eosinophilic and lymphocyte-dominated inflammation, and fibrosis, which were insufficient for a definitive diagnosis. Given concern regarding the radiographic features and clinical progression, surgical excision with bilateral internal jugular vein ligation and free rectus femoris flap reconstruction was performed.

case_info.explanation: C. Tattoo-associated necrotizing granulomatous lymphadenitis Histopathological examination showed reactive lymphoid hyperplasia with extensive necrosis, chronic inflammatory cell infiltration (predominantly lymphocytes and plasma cells), and noncaseating granuloma formation. The histological features of inflammatory emboli in the internal jugular vein are similar with that of cervical lymph nodes (Figure 2). Immunohistochemical staining revealed SMA-positive myofibroblastoma cells, but pan-cytokeratin, IgG4, S-100, SOX10, and CD34 were negative. Acid-fast bacilli staining was negative, and mycobacterium tuberculosis PCR failed to detect mycobacterial DNA. Epstein-Barr virus–encoded RNA staining was negative. These findings collectively supported a diagnosis of necrotizing granulomatous lymphadenitis. Tattooing has emerged as a modern cultural phenomenon associated with personal expression. However, its potential adverse effects, ranging from infections to neoplastic complications, demand heightened clinical awareness. Emerging evidence suggests a possible association between tattoos and malignant neoplasms such as lymphoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and basal cell carcinoma, with a higher incidence observed in tattooed populations.1 Granulomatous reactions to tattoo pigments, typically classified as delayed hypersensitivity responses, manifest histopathologically as granuloma annulare or perforating granulomas confined to tattooed regions.2Clinically, these present as pruritic, erythematous nodules or lichenoid changes, rarely extending into deeper tissues.3Heavy metals (eg, mercury, cadmium) and organic dyes (notably red pigments) in tattoo pigments are implicated in triggering delayed-type hypersensitivity or foreign-body granulomas. While pigment deposition within lesions is a consistent histopathological hallmark, necrosis remains uncommon, with only one other reported case, to our knowledge.4 Lymphatic migration of tattoo pigments may result in lymphadenopathy characterized by painless enlargement and intranodal pigment accumulation, often mimicking metastasis. Imaging modalities such as positron emission tomography–computed tomography frequently fail to differentiate pigment-laden nodes from malignant metastasis, underscoring the necessity of meticulous tattoo history documentation and histopathologic confirmation.5Furthermore, hematogenous dissemination of pigments to distant organs (eg, liver) has been reported, potentially leading to misdiagnosis as metastatic melanoma, particularly in high-risk cohorts.6 Unlike conventional granulomatous reactions, this patient exhibited aggressive local invasion, deep cervical lymphadenopathy, and jugular inflammatory thrombus in the absence of systemic symptoms or infectious etiologies. Thrombus formation in benign inflammatory contexts is previously reported only in association with invasive infections or malignant neoplasms. We propose 3 potential mechanisms: (1) venous wall erosion secondary to granulomatous lymphadenitis, (2) a hypercoagulable state induced by chronic inflammation and cytokine dysregulation (eg, IL-6-mediated fibrinogen production), and (3) vascular stasis due to mass compression by enlarged lymph nodes. This case distinguishes from prior reports of necrotizing granulomas confined to the tattooed skin with minimal deep infiltration. Lymph node involvement preceded local skin reactions, which favored the diagnosis. Notably, red tattoo pigment was absent in resected lesions despite histopathological and clinical correlation supporting the diagnosis. This report expands the spectrum of tattoo-associated pathology. Clinicians should remain highly suspicious of tattoo-related etiologies in patients presenting with necrotic neck masses, even in the absence of visible pigment. Vascular invasion necessitates urgent evaluation, as thrombosis may require immediate intervention. While topical corticosteroid therapy proves ineffective, complete surgical excision remains the cornerstone of both diagnosis and management. The patient finally recovered under the comprehensive treatment mode of surgical operation, short-term systemic hormone therapy, and infection prevention.

case_info.explanation: C. Tattoo-associated necrotizing granulomatous lymphadenitis Histopathological examination showed reactive lymphoid hyperplasia with extensive necrosis, chronic inflammatory cell infiltration (predominantly lymphocytes and plasma cells), and noncaseating granuloma formation. The histological features of inflammatory emboli in the internal jugular vein are similar with that of cervical lymph nodes (Figure 2). Immunohistochemical staining revealed SMA-positive myofibroblastoma cells, but pan-cytokeratin, IgG4, S-100, SOX10, and CD34 were negative. Acid-fast bacilli staining was negative, and mycobacterium tuberculosis PCR failed to detect mycobacterial DNA. Epstein-Barr virus–encoded RNA staining was negative. These findings collectively supported a diagnosis of necrotizing granulomatous lymphadenitis. Tattooing has emerged as a modern cultural phenomenon associated with personal expression. However, its potential adverse effects, ranging from infections to neoplastic complications, demand heightened clinical awareness. Emerging evidence suggests a possible association between tattoos and malignant neoplasms such as lymphoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and basal cell carcinoma, with a higher incidence observed in tattooed populations.1 Granulomatous reactions to tattoo pigments, typically classified as delayed hypersensitivity responses, manifest histopathologically as granuloma annulare or perforating granulomas confined to tattooed regions.2Clinically, these present as pruritic, erythematous nodules or lichenoid changes, rarely extending into deeper tissues.3Heavy metals (eg, mercury, cadmium) and organic dyes (notably red pigments) in tattoo pigments are implicated in triggering delayed-type hypersensitivity or foreign-body granulomas. While pigment deposition within lesions is a consistent histopathological hallmark, necrosis remains uncommon, with only one other reported case, to our knowledge.4 Lymphatic migration of tattoo pigments may result in lymphadenopathy characterized by painless enlargement and intranodal pigment accumulation, often mimicking metastasis. Imaging modalities such as positron emission tomography–computed tomography frequently fail to differentiate pigment-laden nodes from malignant metastasis, underscoring the necessity of meticulous tattoo history documentation and histopathologic confirmation.5Furthermore, hematogenous dissemination of pigments to distant organs (eg, liver) has been reported, potentially leading to misdiagnosis as metastatic melanoma, particularly in high-risk cohorts.6 Unlike conventional granulomatous reactions, this patient exhibited aggressive local invasion, deep cervical lymphadenopathy, and jugular inflammatory thrombus in the absence of systemic symptoms or infectious etiologies. Thrombus formation in benign inflammatory contexts is previously reported only in association with invasive infections or malignant neoplasms. We propose 3 potential mechanisms: (1) venous wall erosion secondary to granulomatous lymphadenitis, (2) a hypercoagulable state induced by chronic inflammation and cytokine dysregulation (eg, IL-6-mediated fibrinogen production), and (3) vascular stasis due to mass compression by enlarged lymph nodes. This case distinguishes from prior reports of necrotizing granulomas confined to the tattooed skin with minimal deep infiltration. Lymph node involvement preceded local skin reactions, which favored the diagnosis. Notably, red tattoo pigment was absent in resected lesions despite histopathological and clinical correlation supporting the diagnosis. This report expands the spectrum of tattoo-associated pathology. Clinicians should remain highly suspicious of tattoo-related etiologies in patients presenting with necrotic neck masses, even in the absence of visible pigment. Vascular invasion necessitates urgent evaluation, as thrombosis may require immediate intervention. While topical corticosteroid therapy proves ineffective, complete surgical excision remains the cornerstone of both diagnosis and management. The patient finally recovered under the comprehensive treatment mode of surgical operation, short-term systemic hormone therapy, and infection prevention.

A 20-year-old man presented with bilateral neck masses that gradually increased in size for over 5 months following a red cross tattoo on his anterior neck. Enhanced computed tomography implied bilateral internal jugular vein thrombosis as well. case_info.explanation: C. Tattoo-associated necrotizing granulomatous lymphadenitis Histopathological examination showed reactive lymphoid hyperplasia with extensive necrosis, chronic inflammatory cell infiltration (predominantly lymphocytes and plasma cells), and noncaseating granuloma formation. The histological features of inflammatory emboli in the internal jugular vein are similar with that of cervical lymph nodes (Figure 2). Immunohistochemical staining revealed SMA-positive myofibroblastoma cells, but pan-cytokeratin, IgG4, S-100, SOX10, and CD34 were negative. Acid-fast bacilli staining was negative, and mycobacterium tuberculosis PCR failed to detect mycobacterial DNA. Epstein-Barr virus–encoded RNA staining was negative. These findings collectively supported a diagnosis of necrotizing granulomatous lymphadenitis. Tattooing has emerged as a modern cultural phenomenon associated with personal expression. However, its potential adverse effects, ranging from infections to neoplastic complications, demand heightened clinical awareness. Emerging evidence suggests a possible association between tattoos and malignant neoplasms such as lymphoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and basal cell carcinoma, with a higher incidence observed in tattooed populations.1 Granulomatous reactions to tattoo pigments, typically classified as delayed hypersensitivity responses, manifest histopathologically as granuloma annulare or perforating granulomas confined to tattooed regions.2Clinically, these present as pruritic, erythematous nodules or lichenoid changes, rarely extending into deeper tissues.3Heavy metals (eg, mercury, cadmium) and organic dyes (notably red pigments) in tattoo pigments are implicated in triggering delayed-type hypersensitivity or foreign-body granulomas. While pigment deposition within lesions is a consistent histopathological hallmark, necrosis remains uncommon, with only one other reported case, to our knowledge.4 Lymphatic migration of tattoo pigments may result in lymphadenopathy characterized by painless enlargement and intranodal pigment accumulation, often mimicking metastasis. Imaging modalities such as positron emission tomography–computed tomography frequently fail to differentiate pigment-laden nodes from malignant metastasis, underscoring the necessity of meticulous tattoo history documentation and histopathologic confirmation.5Furthermore, hematogenous dissemination of pigments to distant organs (eg, liver) has been reported, potentially leading to misdiagnosis as metastatic melanoma, particularly in high-risk cohorts.6 Unlike conventional granulomatous reactions, this patient exhibited aggressive local invasion, deep cervical lymphadenopathy, and jugular inflammatory thrombus in the absence of systemic symptoms or infectious etiologies. Thrombus formation in benign inflammatory contexts is previously reported only in association with invasive infections or malignant neoplasms. We propose 3 potential mechanisms: (1) venous wall erosion secondary to granulomatous lymphadenitis, (2) a hypercoagulable state induced by chronic inflammation and cytokine dysregulation (eg, IL-6-mediated fibrinogen production), and (3) vascular stasis due to mass compression by enlarged lymph nodes. This case distinguishes from prior reports of necrotizing granulomas confined to the tattooed skin with minimal deep infiltration. Lymph node involvement preceded local skin reactions, which favored the diagnosis. Notably, red tattoo pigment was absent in resected lesions despite histopathological and clinical correlation supporting the diagnosis. This report expands the spectrum of tattoo-associated pathology. Clinicians should remain highly suspicious of tattoo-related etiologies in patients presenting with necrotic neck masses, even in the absence of visible pigment. Vascular invasion necessitates urgent evaluation, as thrombosis may require immediate intervention. While topical corticosteroid therapy proves ineffective, complete surgical excision remains the cornerstone of both diagnosis and management. The patient finally recovered under the comprehensive treatment mode of surgical operation, short-term systemic hormone therapy, and infection prevention.

[Case]
A 20-year-old man presented with bilateral neck masses that gradually increased in size for over 5 months following a red cross tattoo on his anterior neck. Three months after the tattoo, the red ink spontaneously faded and was replaced by atrophic scars and necrotic ulcers with light bloody exudation. Initial management with antibiotics and topical corticosteroids yielded no improvement. Physical examination revealed firm, ill-defined cervical and submental lymphadenopathy bilaterally, alongside a midline anterior neck mass demonstrating cutaneous invasion, ulceration, and crusting (Figure 1A). No systemic symptom was observed. Laboratory tests including complete blood cell count, tuberculosis T-cell gamma interferon assay, serum IgG4, and complete immune testing results were within normal limits. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated ill-defined infiltrative masses measuring 3.8 × 2.9 cm and 3.4 × 4.2 cm on both sides of the neck and 4.9 × 3.5 cm in the suprasternal fossa. The lesions showed heterogeneous iso-/hyperintense signal on T1-weighted imaging and hyper-/hypointense signal on T2-weighted imaging, with contrast-enhanced lesions showing predominantly peripheral enhancement. The internal jugular vein in the lower part of the neck was invisible, leaving vague hyperintense signal embedded in the mass (Figure 1B). Enhanced computed tomography implied bilateral internal jugular vein thrombosis as well. Repeated fine-needle aspiration yielded necrotic debris, eosinophilic and lymphocyte-dominated inflammation, and fibrosis, which were insufficient for a definitive diagnosis. Given concern regarding the radiographic features and clinical progression, surgical excision with bilateral internal jugular vein ligation and free rectus femoris flap reconstruction was performed.
